summary.text: A red giant is a luminous giant star of low or intermediate mass, roughly 0.3 to 8 times the Sun's, in a late phase of its evolution.
Its outer atmosphere is inflated, giving a large radius and a surface around 5,000 K or lower, so it looks yellow-white to reddish-orange.
It is many times more luminous than the Sun because of its sheer size, and it usually produces a planetary nebula and becomes a white dwarf.

items.prompt: A red giant's outer layers are cooler than the Sun's surface, yet the star outshines the Sun many times over. Why?

options.label: Its core burns hotter than any other star's
It sits much closer to us than the Sun does
Its enormous size makes up for the cooler envelope
Cool gas gives off more light than hot gas

items.explain: Despite the lower energy density of their envelope, red giants are many times more luminous than the Sun because of their sheer size.

items.prompt: A star has used up the hydrogen in its core, and a shell around the core now fuses hydrogen while the core inside keeps contracting. What happens to the layers outside the shell?

options.label: They expand greatly
They shrink along with the core
They stay exactly the same size
They are pulled into the core

items.explain: Under the mirror principle, when the core within the shell contracts, the layers outside the shell must expand.

items.prompt: One red giant is about the Sun's mass and another is much more massive. Both reach the point of fusing helium in the core. How does the start differ?

options.label: Neither starts; helium fusion never begins
The massive one starts all at once in a flash
Both start in exactly the same way
The Sun-like one starts all at once in a helium flash

items.explain: In Sun-like stars the core becomes degenerate and fuses helium nearly all at once in a helium flash, while in more massive stars helium fusion begins much more smoothly.

items.prompt: Many illustrations draw a red giant with a crisp, sharp edge like a ball. Is that how the real star looks?

options.label: Yes, it has a sharply defined edge
No, it fades gradually into a corona
Yes, but only in the coolest red giants
No, it has no outer layers at all

items.explain: The envelope has a very low mass density, so there is no well-defined photosphere and the star gradually transitions into a corona.

items.prompt: Why do so many of the well-known bright stars in the sky turn out to be red giants?

options.label: They are luminous and moderately common
They are the only stars old enough to be named
They are the closest stars to the Sun
They are the hottest stars in the sky

items.explain: Red giants are luminous and moderately common, so many familiar bright stars are red giants.

items.prompt: The brightness of red giants changes so often. What feature of their surface goes with that?

options.label: A large number of small convection cells
A sharply defined photosphere
A surface hotter than the Sun's
Just a few large convection cells

items.explain: Unlike Sun-like stars with many small solar granules, red-giant photospheres have just a few large cells, which cause the common brightness variations.

paragraphs.heading: An old, swollen star
paragraphs.text: A red giant is a bright, giant star with a low or middle mass, roughly 0.3 to 8 solar masses, that has reached a late stage of its life. It has run through the hydrogen in its core and now fuses hydrogen in a shell around that core instead. Its outer atmosphere has puffed up and thinned out, so its radius is tens to hundreds of times the Sun's and its surface is around 5,000 K or cooler. In colour such stars range from yellow-white to reddish-orange.

paragraphs.heading: Cool but very bright
paragraphs.text: Even though their outer layers are cool, red giants give off many times more energy than the Sun, simply because they are so big. Stars on the red-giant branch reach almost three thousand times the Sun's luminosity, with surfaces of 3,000–4,000 K for types K and M, against nearly 6,000 K for the Sun. Because they are luminous and fairly common, many well-known bright stars are red giants. Arcturus, 36 light-years away, is one, and Gacrux, at 88 light-years, is the nearest M-class giant.

paragraphs.heading: How a star becomes one
paragraphs.text: The Sun spends about 10 billion years on the main sequence, and heavier stars burn their fuel faster and live shorter lives. When the core has mostly used up its hydrogen, its nuclear reactions slow, and so does the outward pressure that held the star up against gravity. The star shrinks and grows hotter inside until a shell around the core is hot enough to fuse hydrogen. The energy from that shell pushes the outer layers outward. The star cools as it swells, a phase called the subgiant stage, and once its envelope starts to convect it stops growing, gets brighter and climbs the red-giant branch.

paragraphs.heading: The mirror principle
paragraphs.text: Astronomers describe what happens around the burning shell as the mirror principle: when the core inside the shell shrinks, the layers outside it must expand. The detailed physics is complex. Still, this behaviour is needed for a star with a shell to conserve both its gravitational and its thermal energy. The core, with no fusion of its own, contracts and heats up, while the outer layers swell hugely and take in most of the extra energy from the shell.

paragraphs.heading: Helium lights up
paragraphs.text: What happens next depends on the star's mass. In the Sun and stars under about 2 solar masses, the core becomes so dense that electron degeneracy pressure stops it from collapsing further. It keeps heating until it reaches roughly 1×10⁸ K, hot enough to fuse helium into carbon through the triple-alpha process, and then the whole core starts fusing helium almost at once in a helium flash. In heavier stars the core reaches that temperature before it becomes degenerate, so helium fusion starts smoothly, with no flash. Stars fusing helium in their cores sit on the horizontal branch if they are poor in metals, or on the red clump if they are rich in them.

paragraphs.heading: No sharp edge, and the end
paragraphs.text: Pictures often give red giants a crisp edge, but real ones do not have one. Their outer envelope is so thin that they lack a clear photosphere, and the star fades gradually into a 'corona'. Their surfaces differ from the Sun's too: instead of many small convection cells, a red giant has just a few large ones, and these cause the changes in brightness so often seen in such stars. At the end of its life, a red giant usually produces a planetary nebula and becomes a white dwarf.
